introduction-it-works-on-my-machine.core: Setup scripts fail because every laptop differs in OS, language versions and system libraries. Declarative environments (Dev Containers, Nix) describe the toolchain as code, so everyone gets the same one.

first_principles.problem: A new hire spends two days fighting 'Python 3.9 required', missing libssl and Homebrew conflicts before writing any code.
truths: Manual setup steps drift from reality.
derivation: **Build** it the same way for everyone.

analogy.title: A meal kit vs. a shopping list
analogy.story: A shopping list leads to different brands and missing items. A meal kit arrives with exactly the ingredients you need.
analogy.breaks: Environments still need maintaining, but the upkeep happens in code instead of in wiki pages.

example.title: Onboarding before and after
example.scenario: Two days down to ten minutes.

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: The first PR lands on day one.

check.q: Why do README setup instructions fail over time?
check.a: Machines and dependency versions drift, and nobody keeps the manual steps in sync.

dev-containers-the-dockerized-ide.core: A Dev Container keeps the editor UI on your machine while tools, runtimes and terminals run inside a container defined by `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`, so everyone shares an identical environment.

first_principles.problem: Different local toolchains produce different lint results, test failures and 'works for me' bugs.
truths: Editors can connect to remote environments.
Config in the repo travels with the code.
derivation: Define the **image or Dockerfile** plus **features** in devcontainer.json.
Open with **'Reopen in Container'** or Codespaces.

analogy.title: A rental workshop
analogy.story: Your hands stay outside (the UI), but every tool and the workbench are inside a fully equipped rental space.
analogy.breaks: It depends on Docker and its resources. File-sync performance on macOS can be slow.

example.title: A Python + Postgres project

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Everyone has Python 3.12, Terraform and the same extensions.

example.outcome: identical dev environments with a click.

points: UI local, tools in the container.

check.q: Where does the code run in a Dev Container setup?
check.a: Inside the container; only the editor UI runs on the host.

nix-the-reproducibility-engine.core: Nix builds every package from a pinned, hashed recipe into an isolated store path, so environments are bit-for-bit reproducible. `apt-get install` in a Dockerfile gives you 'whatever is current today'.

first_principles.problem: Rebuilding the same Dockerfile next month can produce different tool versions, because apt and pip resolve whatever is newest.
truths: Imperative installs depend on when they run.
Hashing all inputs makes builds deterministic.
Isolated store paths allow many versions side by side.
derivation: Packages are **pure functions** of their inputs.
**nix develop** gives a project shell with exactly those tools.

analogy.title: A recipe with exact batch numbers
analogy.story: Not 'some flour', but flour batch #7781 from mill X, so the cake comes out identical every time, anywhere.
analogy.breaks: Nix has a steep learning curve and its own language. Debugging can be hard.

example.title: A project dev shell with a flake

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: `nix develop` gives identical tools now and in a year.

check.q: Why is a Dockerfile with apt-get less reproducible than Nix?
check.a: apt resolves whatever versions are current at build time, while Nix pins every input by hash.

dev-containers-vs-nix-choosing-the-right.core: Dev Containers are easy to adopt and IDE-integrated but less precisely reproducible. Nix is exactly reproducible and runs natively (no VM overhead on macOS), but it's harder to learn. The two can be combined.

first_principles.problem: Teams pick one by hype and then fight its weaknesses.
truths: Exact reproducibility matters more in some contexts.
Mac performance with Docker can hurt.
derivation: **Dev Containers**: quick onboarding, Codespaces, Docker-familiar teams.
**Nix**: exact pins, native speed, polyglot toolchains.
**Both**: Nix inside a Dev Container, or Nix-built images.

analogy.title: A rented furnished flat vs. building with precise blueprints
analogy.story: The flat is ready today. The blueprint build is exact, but you have to learn to read blueprints.
analogy.breaks: Neither replaces CI. Make CI use the same definition for parity.

example.title: Two teams
flow: Web team, mixed skills → Dev Containers + Codespaces
Infra team, many CLIs, Mac → Nix flakes + direnv
Both: CI uses the same definition

steps.label: Principle
steps.detail: Fit the tool to the team and the need for reproducibility.

example.outcome: the environment strategy matches the team.

check.q: When might Nix be preferred over Dev Containers?
check.a: When exact reproducibility and native performance (e.g. on macOS) matter and the team can absorb the learning curve.
